public_rationale: The claim says nobody spending millions on AI tokens can measure the return, and that the cost cannot be predicted. Uber fits it. Its COO said he cannot draw a line from rising Claude Code use to useful features, and Uber used up its 2026 AI coding budget in four months. But one firm cannot prove an 'everybody' or 'nobody' claim. The likeliest counterexample is weak. 8x8 told WIRED in June 2026 that Claude helped it save about $5M a year, more than its Claude bill. That bill may be under the 'millions' threshold, the savings are self-reported, and the report came after the post. I found no clear case before the post of a company spending millions on tokens and publishing a measured return on it, and no evidence that settles the claim either way.
limitations: Sweeping universal wording; only a clear counterexample could settle it.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Everybody spending millions of dollars on AI tokens is experimenting; nobody really knows how to measure AI's ROI, and LLMs' chaotic nature makes it impossible to measure how much it might cost.
conditions: spending millions of dollars on AI tokens

statement.excerpt: Everybody spending millions of dollars on AI tokens is experimenting. As I’ve discussed previously, nobody really knows how to measure the ROI of AI, and the naturally-chaotic nature of LLMs makes it impossible to measure how much it might even cost:

from_speaker: Everybody spending millions of dollars on AI tokens is experimenting
nobody really knows how to measure the ROI of AI
the naturally-chaotic nature of LLMs makes it impossible to measure how much it might even cost
our_interpretation: Plain reading: as of the post, no company spending millions on AI tokens can credibly show a measured return on that spending, and none can reliably predict what its token use will cost.
'Experimenting' is read loosely: spending without an established, measured payoff. It is not read as a formal pilot status.
'How much it might even cost' is read as predicting or budgeting future cost, not metering past spend, since the passage that follows is about budgeting.
He named no period. I use the state around the post: April 1 to May 26, 2026.
criteria.support_condition: Reporting shows large token spenders consistently unable to measure returns or to predict costs, with no credible counterexample.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A company spending millions of dollars a year on AI tokens publicly reports a specific, measured financial return on that spending (savings or profit above its token bill), or shows it can reliably forecast its token costs.

evidence.excerpt: “If you’re not actually able to draw a direct line to how [many] useful features and functionality you’re shipping to your users, that trade becomes harder to justify,” Macdonald said.
evidence.explanation: A large token spender's executive says he cannot link the spending to output. This fits the claim but is one company.

evidence.excerpt: the firm had already burnt through its entire 2026 AI coding tools budget in just four months
evidence.explanation: Uber did not forecast its token costs well. This fits the 'hard to predict cost' reading for one firm.

evidence.excerpt: the company estimates it has saved about $5 million in annual costs by canceling subscriptions to dozens of software and educational tools
evidence.explanation: A company claims a measured saving above its Claude bill. But the bill is only 'well below' $5M, so it may not be a 'millions on tokens' spender. The report is also after the post and self-reported, so it is not decisive.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A company spending millions a year on AI tokens publicly reporting, before or around May 2026, a specific financial return that exceeds its token spend, or systematic evidence that large spenders cannot measure returns.
